Option A - Databases
1. A software company employs programmers and managers.
• Each programmer works on a single project.
• Each project has multiple programmers.
• Each manager oversees multiple projects.
• Each project has one manager.
(a) Construct an entity-relationship diagram (ERD) that shows the relationships
between programmer, manager and project.
(2]
When a programmer changes source code, the changes are automatically written
to a database and timestamped.
(b) Outline one benefit of using a database to track changes to source code.
(2]
(c) Outline the role of timestamps in maintaining data consistency.
[2]
Multiple programmers can work on the same source code concurrently (at the same time).
(d) Explain one way in which concurrency can be managed in the database when two
programmers update the same line of code at the same time.
[5]
(e) When data corruption occurs, databases need to be restored to a consistent state.
(i) Outline what is meant by a consistent database state.
[2]
(ii)
Describe one recovery method that can be used to restore a database.
[3]

practice_questions.question_text: Two clients read version7 of a database row. One commits a change, creating version8. Outline how comparing the saved version before the second update can prevent a lost update.
practice_questions.adaptation_rationale: Original timestamp ordering is narrowed to a supplied version-check mechanism illustrating transaction consistency/isolation; no particular timestamp protocol is required.
practice_questions.solution: The database compares the second client’s saved version7 with current version8. It rejects or retries the stale update rather than overwriting the newer committed data.

practice_questions.question_text: Explain how transaction locking can prevent two clerks from overwriting each other’s edits to the same booking record.
practice_questions.adaptation_rationale: Rebuilt scenario and response wording while retaining the supported reasoning; source-specific obsolete material excluded.
practice_questions.solution: A transaction obtains a suitable exclusive lock before updating the record. A competing writer waits or retries. The first change is committed before the next writer reads and updates the current value. Releasing locks at the appropriate transaction boundary preserves isolation and avoids a lost update.

marking_points.criterion: Update operates on current data in an ordered sequence.

practice_questions.adaptation_rationale: Rebuilt scenario and response wording while retaining the supported reasoning; source-specific obsolete material excluded.
practice_questions.solution: Integrity rules remain satisfied before and after a valid transaction; for example, the combined balance is unchanged when the amount is debited from one account and credited to the other.

practice_questions.question_text: Describe how ROLLBACK can restore a consistent state when an unfinished transfer has debited one account but has not credited the other.

practice_questions.solution: ROLLBACK undoes the uncommitted debit and other changes of that transaction. Both accounts return to their pre-transaction values, avoiding a half-completed transfer.
